title: First Take Something Positive Away
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article argues that the usual response to failure, reviewing what went wrong, neglects the confidence-building step of identifying what went right. Citing coach Don Shula, it says performers should first take something positive from every outing, regardless of the score, and underline the actions worth repeating. Doing so builds confidence and a positive frame of reference so that correcting missteps afterwards feels less debilitating. The author adds that leaders often fail because they face a brand-new challenge and improvise, and that focusing only on errors imprints negative impressions that linger until the next performance. The recommendation is to sequence the debrief, positives first and missteps second, so that errors can be acknowledged without defensiveness.
points: Post-mortems and fail-forward culture focus almost entirely on what went wrong, which aids learning but not confidence.
Shula's point is to underline what went right before turning to errors, not merely to learn from the failure.
Starting with positives creates a positive frame of reference that makes correction feel less debilitating.
Dwelling exclusively on mistakes imprints negative impressions that persist into the next performance.
quotes: While missteps come in many shapes and sizes, the reactions to failure focus almost exclusively on the negative. What went wrong gets all the attention. This aids learning, but not confidence.

In the words of legendary coach Don Shula, “Every time you compete, you must take something positive from it, regardless of the score.” Shula isn’t talking about learning from the failure. Like so many other successful coaches, he means underlining what went right.

By first and foremost focusing on the actions worth repeating, performers build confidence and create a positive frame of reference. Once the positive takeaways have been established, aiming at the missteps and how to correct them doesn’t seem so debilitating.
Leaders who fall flat on their faces in a given situation often do so because the challenge is brand new. Having never seen the problem or situation before, they make things up as they go.
Focusing exclusively on what went wrong, as opposed to what went right, seems logical. But it imprints negative thoughts and impressions that will linger until the next performance.

By taking away the positive first, leaders and team members create a learning climate where errors and mistakes can be acknowledged and rectified without defensiveness. Learning to highlight the positive before turning to missteps is how great performers learn best.
